web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
question: Why do DLF's reported sales, margins, taxes, and cash flows diverge so sharply—and how clean is the balance sheet underneath?

epigraph.quote: In real estate accounting, cash flow is the truth, RERA escrow is the constraint, and the P&L is just the delivery calendar.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Desk Note

web_blocks.caption: DLF Ltd: 10-Year Consolidated Profit & Loss (FY17–FY26 & TTM, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Reported revenue stayed range-bound (₹5,414–₹8,366 Cr) due to Ind AS 115 completion timing, while Interest fell 93% from ₹2,980 Cr (FY17) to ₹199 Cr (FY26) and ₹93 Cr (TTM).

web_blocks.caption: DLF Ltd: 10-Year Consolidated Balance Sheet (Mar 2017–Sep 2026, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Borrowings collapsed from ₹29,202 Cr (Mar 2017) to ₹314 Cr (Sep 2026), while Other Liabilities (largely Ind AS 115 customer advances/contract liabilities) rose from ₹10,623 Cr (Mar 2022) to ₹32,202 Cr (Sep 2026).

web_blocks.caption: DLF Ltd: 10-Year Consolidated Cash Flow Statement (FY17–FY26, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating Cash Flow surged from -₹898 Cr (FY17) and ₹356 Cr (FY20) to ₹5,235 Cr (FY25) and ₹6,347 Cr (FY26), with CFO/EBITDA hitting 254% in FY25 and 484% in FY26.

web_blocks.caption: DLF Ltd: 10-Year Efficiency & Return Ratios (FY17–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: Reported ROCE (6%–7%) and ROE (9.61%) appear optically low because ₹22,947 Cr of Investments (DCCDL JV) and ₹15,084 Cr of cash/RERA balances sit on the balance sheet while ₹60,134 Cr of sold revenue awaits recognition.

web_blocks.title: Five Forensic Deep-Dives Every Analyst Must Check

web_blocks.html: 1. Ind AS 115 Revenue Lag vs. Cash Conversion: Since FY19, DLF has used the completed-contract method under Ind AS 115 [1, 13]. Revenue hits the P&L only after Occupation Certificates arrive and possession is offered [1, 13]. As a result, FY26 Sales grew just 3% YoY to ₹8,194 crore, and TTM Sales dipped to ₹6,375 crore [1]. Q2FY27 OPM also fell to 1.8% on a reported basis [1, 6]. This dip happened because The Camellias is nearly done, with ₹12,135 crore of ₹12,250 crore already booked [6, 9]. Meanwhile, The Arbour, Privana, and The Dahlias hold over ₹54,000 crore in sales but have not reached handover [6, 9]. Buyer advances flow straight into Other Liabilities, which tripled from ₹10,623 crore in FY22 to ₹32,202 crore in Sep 2026 [1]. That cash lifted Operating Cash Flow to ₹6,347 crore, or 484% of operating profit [1].

2. Other Income & One-Time Valuation Gains: Screener shows Other Income of ₹1,825 crore in FY26 and ₹2,069 crore on a TTM basis [1]. That equals 62%–74% of PBT [1]. A closer look reveals two parts [6, 22]. The first is steady interest earned on ₹15,084 crore of cash and RERA balances, yielding ₹156 crore in Q2FY27 alone [6]. The second is non-operating fair-value gains, such as the ₹738 crore one-time gain on Atrium Place JV stakes in Q2FY27 [6, 22]. Analysts should strip out fair-value gains when modelling core profit.

3. Why Net Profit Exceeds PBT & Tax Rate Anomalies: In FY26, Consolidated Net Profit (₹4,415 crore) topped Profit Before Tax (₹2,932 crore) [1]. Effective tax rates also swung from -19% in FY25 to +11% in FY26 [1]. Two structural items explain this gap [1, 6]. First, DLF's 66.67% share of DCCDL net profit is added after PBT as 'Share of Profit from Associates/JVs' [1, 6]. DCCDL posted ₹2,721 crore PAT in FY26 and gave DLF a ₹499 crore share in Q2FY27 alone [6]. Second, DLF used deferred tax assets and legacy tax credits [1, 6]. As residential handovers surge from FY28 onward, cash tax rates should settle near ~25%.

4. RERA 70% Escrow Ring-Fencing (Restricted vs. Free Cash): DLF held ₹15,084 crore in cash on September 30, 2026, up from ₹14,155 crore in FY26 [6]. Yet ₹12,270 crore (81%) sits inside RERA 70% project escrow accounts [6]. By law, DLF can spend those funds only on land and build costs for each registered project [9, 13]. It cannot use escrow cash to pay dividends or buy unrelated land [9, 13]. Free corporate cash is roughly ₹2,814 crore [6]. That is still ample against ₹314 crore of gross debt and is backed by ₹420 crore/quarter in DCCDL dividends [1, 6]. Still, free cash is much smaller than the headline figure.

5. Off-Balance-Sheet DCCDL Leverage: Parent DLF Limited is nearly debt-free with just ₹314 crore in gross debt [1, 6]. However, its 66.67%-owned JV DCCDL holds ₹18,420 crore of net debt against ₹99,640 crore of Gross Asset Value [6]. That puts Net Debt/GAV at 18%, down from 26% in FY23 [6]. DCCDL's Net Debt/EBITDA improved from 4.5x in FY23 to 3.0x–3.1x at a 7.04% exit interest rate [6]. This earned CRISIL and ICRA AAA/Stable ratings [6]. Even so, investors must count JV debt on a look-through basis rather than treating the whole group as debt-free.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Verdict on Accounting Quality
paragraphs: DLF uses conservative Ind AS 115 revenue rules and posts strong cash flow (₹6,347 Cr FY26 CFO; ₹6,231 Cr FCF) [1, 6]. It has zero promoter-pledge stress and AAA-rated JV debt [1, 6]. For clean analysis, make two adjustments [6, 22]. First, strip one-time JV fair-value gains out of Other Income [6, 22]. Second, note that 81% of cash is locked in RERA escrow for active builds [6].

book_paragraphs: If you only glance at DLF's ten-year profit and loss table, you might walk away confused. Revenue barely budged between 2015 and 2026, sitting around ₹5,500 crore to ₹8,200 crore a year. Operating margins dipped to eighteen percent in fiscal 2026 and under two percent in a single recent quarter. Yet over that same stretch, operating cash flow exploded to ₹6,347 crore, free cash flow hit ₹6,231 crore, and net profit climbed above ₹4,400 crore. How can both be true at the same time?

The answer lies in five forensic details that every serious investor must unpack. First is Ind AS 115, India's completed-contract accounting rule. Since fiscal 2019, DLF has been barred from booking residential sales as revenue until a building receives its occupation certificate and keys are handed over. Right now, The Camellias is almost finished, while The Arbour, Privana, and The Dahlias are still rising out of the ground. So customer deposits pour into cash flow today—pushing customer advances on the balance sheet from ₹10,623 crore in March 2022 to ₹32,202 crore in September 2026—while the revenue waits until fiscal 2028 and beyond.

Second is Other Income. In fiscal 2026, Other Income reached ₹1,825 crore, and over the trailing twelve months it topped ₹2,069 crore—nearly three-quarters of pre-tax profit. Part of that is genuine interest earned on DLF's huge cash pile, such as ₹156 crore in a single recent quarter. Another part, like the ₹738 crore valuation gain on Atrium Place in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, is a one-time accounting mark-up. Always separate recurring interest from one-off gains.

Third is why reported net profit of ₹4,415 crore in fiscal 2026 actually exceeded pre-tax profit of ₹2,932 crore, and why the tax rate turned negative in fiscal 2025 and stayed at just eleven percent in fiscal 2026. That happens because DLF's two-thirds share of DCCDL's profit is added below the pre-tax line, alongside deferred tax credits. As residential handovers surge later this decade, cash tax rates should drift back toward twenty-five percent.

book_subsections.title: The Two Balance-Sheet Traps to Avoid
paragraphs: First, do not treat DLF's ₹15,084 crore cash balance as free money sitting in a checking account. Roughly ₹12,270 crore of that cash—over eighty-one percent—is locked inside project-specific RERA escrow accounts. By law, DLF can only spend that money to finish the exact towers those buyers paid for. Unrestricted corporate cash is closer to ₹2,814 crore, which is still very healthy against just ₹314 crore of corporate borrowings and supported by ₹420 crore quarterly dividends from DCCDL, but much smaller than the headline number.

Second, remember the debt sitting inside DCCDL. While DLF's parent balance sheet is virtually debt-free—with interest expense down ninety-three percent from ₹2,980 crore in fiscal 2017 to ₹199 crore in fiscal 2026—the commercial joint venture carries ₹18,420 crore of net debt against nearly ₹1,00,000 crore of prime offices and malls. At three times EBITDA and an average interest rate near seven percent, that debt is triple-A rated and conservative, but it is still leverage you should count when looking at the whole group.

book_subsections.title: Why Return on Equity Looks Low on Paper
paragraphs: You may also notice that DLF's ten-year return on capital employed sits at six to seven percent and return on equity sits near ten percent. Do not mistake that for a weak business. Those ratios look low because ₹22,947 crore of commercial investments and ₹15,084 crore of cash sit on the asset base today while ₹60,134 crore of already-sold homes have not yet been allowed onto the income statement. Once completions accelerate after fiscal 2028, reported returns on capital will look very different.

book_callouts.title: Cash Flow vs. Escrow Reality
book_callouts.text: DLF's ₹6,347 crore FY26 operating cash flow is real, but ₹12,270 crore of its ₹15,084 crore cash pile is legally ring-fenced inside RERA 70% accounts to finish sold homes.
